ANNEX

A

( Foreword )
COMMONLY

USED RESINS/REACTANTS AND ADVANTAGES DISADVANTAGES OF UREA-FORMALDEHYDE RESIN

AND

A-l A large number of resins/reactants are available in the market, each one having some advantages and disadvantages. In India, these are mainly based on the following five chemical types: a) b) Methyl01 urea, popularly known as ureaformaldehyde resin ( UF ); ( Tri ) Methylol Melamine, popularly known as melamine-formaldehyde resin ( MF ); ( Di) Methyl01 Ethylene known as DMEU resin; Urea, popularly

c) d) e)

( Di ) Methyl01 Dihydroxy Ethylene Urea, popularly known as DMDHEU resin; and ( Di ) Methyl01 Ethyl Triazone, known as triazonc resin ( DMET popularly ).

A-3 The most widely used resins for imparting wash-and-wear properties to textile fabrics are based on urea-formaldehyde adducts inspite of stiff competition from other resins/reactions. The advantages of urea-formaldehyde adducts are the low cost and high efficiency. Their main drawbacks are the poor stability of the product, poor durability of the finish towards laundering and susceptibility of the fiuished fabric to rlllorine damage after hypochlo~ ite bleaching. The ureaformaldehyde resins are, therefore, recommended only for finishing coloured goods which are not subjected to hypochlorite bleaching during laundering. Urea-forma!dehyde resins are not suitable for post-cure ( also called the deferred cure ) finishing process because the resin cures very easily and the treated fabric would not remain in the sensitized or uncured state for a long time. A-4 Among the quality control tests of resins, one of the most important is obviously the performance test. However, it is rather dilhcult to spell out the exact improvement/deterioration of the properties for given level of treatment mainly because it clppends upon :: number of variables which differ from mill to mill ~IKI fi,on-1 time to lime. For example, the nature oi fabric aucl the pretrea.trnent it has receivctl; quality and quantity of catalyst used in trc`atmcnt; trthcr XccJIIlpmying ausilial ic.s buch as sof~eu~rs: l/T-T of the ]:a&bath; ir:.ati~lg tc~chrliqu~: and condilionz used irlclucling \\<`i:,ic Ii up, i!Iy'lI< nllfl l)ac~l;in~!/,uring ~~IIl~J~~itIl:ir, tinlc, pO(:i S.; w:rsli ard tupj.~ill,~ c,llcinirals etc.

A-2 The resins/reactants are mainly used in durable press finishing of garments, wash-andwear finishing or easy care finishing ot textile fabrics. The treatment with these resins/reactants wet wrinkleimproves dry wrinkle-resistance, property, drip-dry smooth-drying resistancr, property, elasticity, dimensional stability, fastness of many dycstuf'fs, hand and drape 01 fabrics. There is a reduction in tensile strength ( rayons gain ) somewhat in dry strength and substantially in wet strength up to cert:rin level of irPatn~ent., tear strength, abrasion rcsi:,t::nccb, muistult: regain water imbibition, plasticity, flexibility, extensibility and elongation properties.

E-3.1 Weigh accurately about 0.5 g of the sample in a weighing bottle and transfer it to Kjeldahl flask. Add to it 25 ml of concentrated sulphuric acid and 0.5 g of sucrose.
E-3.2 Kerp the Kjeldahl flask in a boiling water bath for one hour and then add 0.1 g selenium, 18 g potassium sulphate and 0.3 g of copper sulphate. Keep the flask in an inclined position and close with a loosely fitting pear shaped hollow glass stopper to prevent loss of sulphuric acid or entry of dust. IIeat the mixture gently in a fume cupboard until the initial frothing has ceased. Heat the liquid to boiling point and continue boiling until the solution becomes clear. Boil the liquid for a further period of' 2 hours and then cool the contents of the flask. E-3.3 Transfer the contents of K.jeldahl flask to a 100-ml volumetric flask and make the solution up to the mark. Takr 10 ml of this solution in a volumetric flask and add to it a few pieces of pumice stone.
